memories.memory_text: I was running through the alley, blood in the snow, barely able to move—my shoulder torn open, every breath sharp—then I pressed into the shadows as police cars screamed past, blue lights flashing, and when they were gone, I forced myself up and staggered toward a pharmacy.
I see '415' on a building. A voice says, 'Welcome to the program.' I'm walking down a corridor, and someone is leading me.

A black sack is thrown over my head, and then I see flashes—kills piling up: the Professor, Jarda, the blonde in Paris, the Neski couple—then Adrian Monroe, her head snapping back from the shot, the car plunging into the water.
I stood at the door of Remy Adler's apartment, and when he opened it, I saw the weight of everything in his eyes—the loss, the anger, the silence we both carried since Adrian Monroe died.
I told Remy Adler his sister was dead, that she was shot because a man came for me — and I knew then I couldn't keep running, not when someone had started all of this.

I was reading the article in The Guardian when I saw her photo—Adrian Monroe, smiling at me like that, and then suddenly it wasn't the paper anymore, it was her face changing, her body jerking from the shots.
After seeing her die again in my head, I was back in that room, setting fire to her clothes, her things—watching everything burn, just like I did to make sure nothing tied her to me.
I called Cameron Reeves from a payphone, told him to meet me at Harborview Hospital, and said my name—'This is Kendall Prescott'—knowing it was the first time I’d spoken it aloud to anyone in years.
I moved with the flow of commuters, stepped close behind Cameron Reeves, and slipped the the red radio into his pocket as I passed—his jacket brushed my hand, and he never saw me.
I heard him answer the the red radio, that pause when he realized it wasn’t his—I spoke before he could react, voice calm but firm, taking control without revealing myself.
I saw a London the weathered key coming from the left and a kid in a hoodie heading to the the weathered key stop on the right—immediately knew I could use them to vanish.

I saw Cameron Reeves spot the target in the blue hoodie, who walked to the the weathered key stop, sat down, and checked his watch. Cameron Reeves shifted nervously. I told him to go to the the weathered key stop, sit next to the man, and keep his head down. Then Cameron Reeves began to move.

I watched from a distance as Cameron Reeves moved through the crowd, seconds ticking—tight window to extract her clean. I told her to take the footbridge, head to the West Entrance, meet me at the newsstand. One chance to get it right.
I came down the stairs and took out the operative in three quick moves before he could react, leaving him slumped against the wall like a drunk.
I pulled the feed and took the earbud, then followed Cameron Reeves while listening to the chaos I'd caused from an ocean away.

I pressed Cameron Reeves about how he knew details about Silverline Police, demanding the name of his source, and when he mentioned 'Westfield Collective'—a name I'd never heard before—I knew it was tied to me, but I didn't understand how.
I saw the operatives approaching, weapons concealed but moving with tactical precision, and immediately knew we were out of time—I had to move Cameron Reeves before they closed in.
I told Cameron Reeves to move toward the news kiosk, guiding him through the commuters before realizing the cameras were shifting.
I told Cameron Reeves to stop and tie his shoelace just as the tourists passed by, using their movement to break the CCTV's line of sight.
I saw the departures board flash Platform 7 and triggered the crowd surge, watching commuters flood forward and push the Westhaven Station back.

After Tristan Vaughn showed me the 'Lethal Action Protocol' and insisted it was legal, I told him Nico Rivers was one of our own and stormed out, unable to stay in the room as he authorized the kill order.

I remember the moment Harper Delaney walked in and said Kendall Prescott and Nico Rivers were dead—his voice flat, no emotion. I just asked if it was confirmed, and when he said not yet, I knew I had to act before the truth was buried.
I opened a new file—Kendall Prescott's operations. It needed to be documented, properly, for the record.

I looked at the faces Kendall Prescott remembered—his kills—and matched them with names, records, the reasons they were targeted. For the first time, I saw the full weight of what Silverline Police did, not as operations, but as people erased.

I found the notation in Kendall Prescott's file—recruited by Owen Warren, inducted at a facility on 71st Westhaven House in Westhaven Station, now closed. The details were buried, but they pointed to a deliberate erasure.

I set down my pencil and said Kendall Prescott's name—just his name—after the the red radio rang. I didn't know yet if this was a trap or a break, but the moment felt sharp, still.
I stood in my office and told Kendall Prescott he was owed an apology—my voice was steady, but the weight of it pressed down like a silence I couldn't ignore.

I spotted an open office down the hall, rushed in, and began faxing the Westfield Collective documents from the black jacket—no time to hesitate.

I remember snapping at the Valerie Finch, pacing, needing that text—then finally seeing it flash on screen: 'Tudor City Pl & 42nd. Ten minutes. Come alone. Come on foot.' The moment it hit, I ordered every unit to surround the area and mobilized the trucks.
I see Remy Quincy standing on the corner, waiting—probably for Kendall Prescott. I need to know if he's anywhere near her, now.

I answered the the red radio and heard Kendall Prescott's voice—cold, controlled—and for a second I couldn't react, then I looked out at the streets, scanning for him, wondering how he got my number and whether he was already watching me.
